Elmwood Disposable Disposal Initiative. Thank you, Madam Chair. This report outlines the results
of the 2025 Elmwood Disposal Initiative, which was implemented in response to the increasing cases
of Dutch Elm Disease. In 2025, Saskatoon recorded 41 confirmed cases up from 11 in 24 and just
4 in 2023. To reduce barriers to proper Elmwood Disposal and slow the spread of the disease,
the city weighed all landfill tipping and entrance fees for residential and commercial Elmwood
in 2025. This approach led to significant increases in proper disposal with nearly 2,000 tons of
Elmwood received at the landfill more than double the volume from the previous year,
demonstrating a strong uptake of the program and improved public compliance.
Survey data from 2025 shows that public awareness and behavior around Elmwood Disposal
improved compared to 2022. More residents understood that Elmwood must be disposed of immediately
and that it cannot be burned or stored and fewer people identified landfill costs or a volume of
material as barriers. However, the survey did identify some ongoing challenges,
including limited access to vehicles for transport and continued improper placement of Elmwood
in residential waste carts, particularly in the green carts. While this initiative has supported
Dutch Elm Disease Prevention, the increased volume of Elmwood Disposed exceeded projections
and resulted in higher than anticipated operational costs at the landfill.
Financially, the program exceeded its approved capital budget in 2025 by 168,800 due to higher
disposal volumes and operational demands. The report this morning recommends re-allocating funding
from existing capital reserves specifically waste reduction initiatives and the urban forestry
and pest management capital reserve to address this over expenditure without impacting landfill
operations. Looking ahead, the report identifies risks to landfill capacity and operating budgets
if elevated Elmwood Disposal volumes continue in 2026 and 2027. We will continue to closely monitor
both and report back if any changes are required. Madam Chair, that's my introduction and if there's
any questions we can respond. Thank you. Great, thank you. To start, can I have someone move the

the forthcoming climate action strategy. Since buildings emit about 59% or 3.3 million tons of
our community's carbon pollution, 59% of those emissions were from the industrial, commercial,

benefits like lower energy costs for property owners and tenants. Improved comfort and safety
for building occupants, increased property value, creating jobs, and improving resilience to climate change.
Next slide, please. This program has been developed through a multi-year feasibility and design
process. Council first approved funding in 2021 to undertake a feasibility and engagement process.
This, the findings from this was brought to Council in 2024. Council then approved a $25 million
internal loan, as well as some core assumptions for the program design. Bringing us to today's report,
where we are requesting approval on the final design. Next slide, please. To design the program,
administration considered the core assumptions completed additional best practice and engagement,
updated the triple bottom line assessment, and used all of these to recommend the final
design parameters. Next slide, please. The previously approved core assumptions are found in
table 1 of appendix 1 in your report. They established the base program design and included the total
funding for help and help. How to set the interest rates, the target and prioritize participants,
the program administrative model, the expectation to break even financially using a 1.6%
administration fee, and setting a $1.5 million max loan amount with an up to 20 year term,
as well as 20% energy targets. Next slide, please. The recommended program design elements are included
as appendix 2 of your report, with more detailed rationale in section 6 of appendix 1.
The program design aims to remove barriers and to encourage energy efficiency upgrades for commercial
building owners, while prioritizing equity and providing financial and legal safeguards for the city.
Some of the recommended design elements include that existing buildings up to 10,000 square meters are
eligible, with priority given to small and medium size buildings, non-profit organizations and affordable
housing providers. New construction is not recommended to be eligible. To be eligible, participants
will need to have all property taxes paid, insurance in place, and have no unresolved leans or foreclosures.
Program applicants must be the legal property owners or authorized representatives. They must be current
on property secured debt, and will need to obtain written consent from their mortgage lender.
Loans up to 1.5 million, or 20% of assessed property value per building. Loan terms will be flexible
at 5 to 20 years and aligned with the effective useful life or EUL of the upgrade. Loans are paid back
through property taxes, with interest rates equal to the city's investment return.
Edmund fees will be aligned with help for small loans under 40,000, and then 1.6% on the amount
above 40,000. Non-profit and affordable housing providers will have the first $750 waived,
and fees reduced to 1% for the amount above 40,000. A lien will be placed on the property,
giving the most municipality first priority in case of default. Note that defaults are historically
very low or no. Next slide, please. To measure and verify performance, most projects will
require an astray level 2 energy audit, and a business case that demonstrates home minimum 20%
energy reduction can be achieved. Completed projects will be verified through permits,
completion certificates, invoices and photos, and disclosure through the benchmarking,
labeling, and disclosure, or BLD tool. The eligible measures include energy and water efficiency,
renewable energy, resilience upgrades, safety remediation, EV charges, and some incidentals.
Next slide, please. The kelp financial analysis is founded in table 1 of the report.
The total loan capital available is 16.6 million, to be loaned out to about 22 building owners
and repayed through property taxes with interest. The program aims to be revenue neutral,
with revenue sources including admin fees, the FCM grant, reallocation of capital from original funding

1 million, including program administration, marketing education, engagement, software, enhancements,
